title: Minimax Precision of Cluster Trials under Exact Participant Quotas with Unequal Cluster Sizes
banked_reason: Stage 0.5 BELOW NOVELTY FLOOR: mathematically sound subfield contribution, ceiling 6.7 below field threshold 7.4; not salvageable in the current tuned two-stratum scope.
gap_reasons: The delivered results establish the fixed-k plateau through an all-design, full-record converse and heterogeneous-table attainment, and establish the matching one-person rescue constant; independent rational replay confirms the L2 enclosure. Their significance is confined to the specified two-stratum arithmetic sequence, with no characterization for general cluster-size vectors or additionally filtered assignment pools. Relative to the public unrestricted results of [Hull](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.09812v3) and [Sudijono et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.13822v1), the contribution is the quota-preserving transfer and discontinuity; slack saturation follows by nesting, and the iterated constant uses classical binomial bounds. The projected score is constrained by this narrow geometry, the computationally impractical general evaluator, and the absence of quantitative finite-trial calibration beyond the small certificates. The framing accurately distinguishes first-order sharpness from the open finite-population correction, so there is no stale matched or second-order overclaim. DeRouen–Mitchell's inaccessible published theorem text remains a scalar-priority source-verification item, but no load-bearing proof step depends on it. banked-comparator-omitted@thm:unrestricted-rescue-saturation: Position the unrestricted first-order saturation theorem against accepted-bank exp_multiarm_secondorder_minimax_frontier_v1: explain that its fixed-K unrestricted response-type minimax frontier is not the present unequal-size cluster hard-quota experiment, and state precisely why the quota-induced plateau and one-person rescue are new rather than leaving this nearest in-repository minimax comparator unaddressed.
proof_attempt_summary: Discovery derived the full-record exact-quota plateau and the sharp one-person rescue, then strengthened the first-order headline to unrestricted and arbitrary-slack saturation. The mathematical panel and independent validity consult found the argument sound, but the achieved subfield tier and 6.7 paper-score ceiling did not meet the field floor; broader cluster-size or filtered-pool characterization requires a new kernel. The finite-population correction remains open, scalar-priority verification and one comparator-positioning omission remain disclosed, and no Lean formalization was attempted.
tldr: Almost equal cluster sizes can make exact participant equality prevent consistent estimation of the person average treatment effect. Optimizing the assignment law and every Borel randomized estimator of the full labeled binary record yields a positive fixed-\(k\) risk limit \(L_k\), the value of an unequal-binomial mean experiment derived through a common table prior and a uniform reconstruction bound. Allowing one participant of imbalance collapses risk to \((1+o(1))/(2G)\), exactly the unrestricted first-order minimax constant; every larger deterministic participant allowance has the same first-order constant, so precision saturates after the first participant. Certified rational calibration evaluates the plateau, including \(L_1=27/256\), the narrow enclosure for \(L_2\), and the iterated constant \(1/8\). Exhaustive fixed-count and arm-total filters instantiate the attaining laws under stated conditions. The finite-population correction remains an open second-order question.
gap: Unrestricted bounded-outcome design theorems use assignment laws outside a hard participant quota. Unequal-size cluster analysis identifies the person target but does not determine precision after optimizing all quota-feasible procedures.
fill: An original-record lower comparison valid before choosing any feasible design, a heterogeneous-individual-table decoder, a sharp rescue constant, and certified calibration of their common scalar limit.
